questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 1
questions.prompt: What is the main job of a constructor?
choices: Establish a valid starting state
Delete the object
Make every member public
Run after every method
questions.explanation: The constructor initializes the new object so its public operations can rely on a valid state.

questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 2

It makes the returned integer constant forever
It hides the method
It allocates the object

questions.title: Trace Classes & Objects
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The constructor initializes the balance, deposit changes it through a rule, and the const getter reads it without modifying the object. The resulting output is '25'.

questions.title: Classes & Objects practice 5
questions.prompt: In this class, why is `balance_` under `private` while `deposit` and `balance` are `public`?
choices: So the balance can only change through methods that enforce the class's rules
So the balance uses less memory than a public field
So the balance is shared across every Account object
So the class compiles faster
questions.explanation: A private field cannot be assigned from outside the class, so no caller can write `account.balance_ = -50`. Every change has to go through `deposit`, which is the one place that can reject an invalid amount. Access level is about who may change the data, not about memory, sharing, or compile speed.

questions.title: Member initializer list
questions.prompt: Why does C++ often prefer a member initializer list for constructor setup?
choices: It initializes members before the constructor body runs, which matters for const members and members without default constructors.
Store all object state in one shared global variable.
Skip constructors and fill fields only when remembered later.
Use a class when no related data or behavior is being grouped.
questions.explanation: Data members are initialized before the constructor body starts. A member initializer list lets the class give each member its starting value at the right moment, instead of default-initializing first and assigning later.

questions.title: One responsibility
questions.prompt: What makes a C++ class easier to understand?
choices: Let outside code change every field directly.
Give the class one clear responsibility.
Put unrelated responsibilities into one large class.
Forget that each object has its own instance data.
questions.explanation: A class with one clear responsibility keeps related state and behavior together without becoming a catch-all. That makes invariants easier to protect and methods easier to name.

questions.title: Initialize every member
questions.prompt: What should a constructor do for the object's data members?
choices: Name methods after vague actions such as `doStuff`.
Use local variables when persistent object state is needed.
Initialize every member in the constructor.
Call an instance method before creating an object.
questions.explanation: Every member should start in a known valid state. Uninitialized members can carry unpredictable values, and later methods may accidentally trust those values as real state.

questions.title: Protect invariants
questions.prompt: Why keep important object state behind private data?
choices: Treat the class blueprint as the same thing as one object.
Leave an object in a half-initialized state.
Make every method change object state even when it should only read.
Keep invariants behind private data.
questions.explanation: Private data lets the class control how its state changes. Public methods can enforce rules, such as keeping a balance nonnegative or a size consistent with stored values.

questions.title: Const methods
questions.prompt: When should a C++ member function be marked `const`?
choices: Mark read-only methods const.
Use static/shared data for per-object information.
Ignore invariants that should stay true after each method call.
Mix user input directly into every object method.
questions.explanation: Mark a member function `const` when it promises not to change the observable state of the object. That promise helps callers use const objects safely and helps the compiler catch accidental mutation.

questions.title: Type design
questions.prompt: What should a well-designed C++ type keep together?
choices: Return internal mutable data without control.
Design types that keep related state and behavior together.
Use inheritance where a helper field would be clearer.
Hide important setup in unrelated methods.
questions.explanation: A type should group the state and behavior that belong to one concept. That makes the object's rules live near the data they protect instead of spreading related logic across unrelated functions.
